fix(llm): stop printLlmLines dropping the blank lines read counts

Review follow-up. `read --format llm` frames its payload with
`content lines=<n>` and then prints the raw source, but printLlmLines skipped
falsy entries -- and a blank source line is `""`. So the header counted lines
that never reached stdout, and a consumer honouring the count read the
following records as source.

Wrong on almost every real input, not an edge case: `ix read src/cli/llm.ts
--format llm` declared 91 and emitted 81. Correct only for a file with no
blank lines and no trailing newline.

`!= null` rather than truthiness. printLlmLines had no callers on main before
this branch, so nothing else is affected: every renderer builds lines with a
record kind, and llmLine returns `""` only for a null kind with no surviving
fields, which no caller passes.

The existing test asserted renderReadLlm's return value, which is correct in
isolation -- the defect was in render composed with print. So outputResult is
exported and the new tests drive the real print path across blank lines, an
empty file, CRLF, no trailing newline, and blank-lines-only.

Also pins doctor's status precedence for {ok:true, warn:true} -- the one shape
the ternary ordering decides, and previously uncovered. It renders `ok`, which
is what the glyph line renders for the same record.

Bug restored on both: 6 targeted failures, then byte-exact restore (sha256
verified). tsc/eslint/knip clean, 667 tests pass.

fix(ingest): resolve JS and TS calls across parse batches

Pre-scan JavaScript and TypeScript definitions into the repository-wide
resolution index so streamed parse batches resolve calls to imported symbols
defined in later batches.

The index derives these from real parse results rather than a regex, so they
cannot drift from what the in-batch path extracts. That costs one parse per
prescanned file, which was a synchronous main-thread loop — fine for R and SAS,
not for .ts, where it is most of a repository and an incremental map pays it for
every unchanged file too.

So the CLI now parses prescan sources on the worker pool it already runs for the
streaming loop and hands the results to buildGlobalResolutionIndex, which uses
them in place of parsing. Measured on this repo (180 JS/TS files), the index
build drops from 1.24s of blocked main thread to 1ms, with the parsing itself
moved onto the pool and spread across cores. Callers without a pool — tests,
library use — still parse in the index exactly as before.

fix(ingest): do not let map mode delete the chunks it cannot rewrite

Three fixes on top of the deletion reconciliation.

1. `ix map` was destroying chunk data. stripMapModeOps drops every chunk
   UpsertNode from the patch but leaves DeleteNode alone, and chunk ids hash
   the chunk's start line — so any edit that shifts lines makes every
   downstream chunk look removed. Running `ix map` after an `ix ingest`
   therefore deleted the file's chunks and never recreated them: the cheap
   command silently destroying what the expensive one built. Chunks are not
   map mode's to reconcile, so reconcileRemovedEntities now takes a mapMode
   flag and leaves chunk nodes and CONTAINS_CHUNK/NEXT edges alone. The kind
   comes from the entity lookup already being made for incident edges, so it
   costs nothing extra.

2. Restored the empty-baseline guard, scoped. An empty mtime map is normally
   a discovery failure — an over-broad ignore rule, the wrong cwd — and
   persisting it discards the baseline and forces a full re-ingest. Dropping
   the guard outright to support "deleted the last file" made every such
   failure destructive. It now asks why the map is empty: with deletions
   recorded, empty is real; without them, discovery is assumed to have gone
   wrong.

3. Scoped the fail-closed hash lookup. Deleting from an unreliable baseline
   is how data gets lost, so failing closed there is right — but letting the
   throw escape aborted the whole map over one transient blip, taking the
   ordinary ingest of every changed file with it. The deletions are now
   dropped for that run and retried next time; the rest proceeds.

fix(php): resolve nullable types and plain-function parameters

The receiver-type queries matched `named_type` only. `?Service` is not one --
tree-sitter-php wraps it as `(optional_type (named_type (name)))` -- so every
nullable dependency fell back to a bare method name. In modern PHP that is most
of them, which made the feature miss the common case rather than an edge one.

Same shape in the parameter query, rooted at `method_declaration`: a top-level
`function run(Service $svc)` is a `function_definition`, a different node, so
its parameters were never typed at all.

Both fixed by accepting `optional_type` alongside `named_type` and alternating
the parameter pattern over both declaration nodes. No handler change was needed
-- `childForFieldName('name')` works on `function_definition`, and with no
enclosing class the scope becomes the bare function name, which is what
`findEnclosingFunction` already returns for one.

Union types are deliberately still bare: a union has no single receiver type to
attribute the call to, so an arbitrary pick of one member would be worse than
the honest fallback. Pinned with a test so it reads as intent, not omission.

Three regression tests; the two for the fixed gaps fail without this change.

fix(cli): register a Pro stub for `goals`

@ix/pro registers a plural list command alongside each singular manager
— bug/bugs, plan/plans, task/tasks, goal/goals — and PRO_COMMANDS stubs
every one of those pairs except the last. `goal` was stubbed; `goals`
was not.

So on an OSS install `ix goals` fell through to commander and printed
`error: unknown command 'goals'`. CLAUDE.md tells agents that a Pro-gated
install is identified by the exact string `The '<name>' command requires
Ix Pro.`, and to stop retrying once they see it. An unrecognized
commander error gives them nothing to match, so the documented contract
simply did not hold for this one command.

This is only reachable from outside the OSS docs, which consistently say
`ix goal list` — but `ix goals` is a real, fully implemented Pro command,
so anyone who learned it on a Pro install, or any plugin that calls it,
hits the wrong error.

The regression test now walks the singular/plural pairs explicitly rather
than listing commands one at a time, since listing is what let this one go
missing.

fix(windows): make the ix.cmd launcher diagnose its own broken target

`ix upgrade` before 0.9.0 refreshed only the bash shim under Git Bash and
left `%IX_HOME%\bin\ix.cmd` aimed at a `cli\ix.cmd` that the same upgrade
had just replaced with a version-nested directory. Everyone upgrading from
<=0.8.1 on Windows lands there, and all cmd.exe offers is

  '"[local-path]"' is not recognized as an internal or
  external command, operable program or batch file.

which names the wrapper rather than the cause and reads like a broken
install rather than a broken upgrade.

This cannot be fixed forward. `ix upgrade` is executed by the version being
upgraded *from*, so no change shipped today reaches the installs that break
— and once broken, `ix doctor` is exactly as unreachable as `ix`. The
recovery instruction therefore has to live in the batch file itself, which
is the only thing the user can still run.

So the launcher now checks its target first and, when it is gone, prints
what happened and the reinstall one-liner. It also propagates %errorlevel%
on the success path, which the old one-line body silently swallowed --
every non-zero ix exit had been reported to callers as success.

install.ps1 and refreshLaunchers() both emit this body; a test asserts the
two stay identical, since they drifting apart is how the flat/nested shim
bugs happened before.

`ix doctor` gains a Windows-only launcher check. It cannot help the
PowerShell user whose shim is dead, but the bash shim IS refreshed by every
version, so someone living in Git Bash can be broken in PowerShell for
weeks without knowing; this tells them.

Refs #385.

fix(view): keep "absent" and "unreadable" apart, and screen the rev at its source

Review of the first commit found three regressions in it, all one mistake:
replacing the `existsSync` guards with bare `catch {}` made an unreadable
file indistinguishable from a missing one. Both callers of `readAlivePid`
treat null as licence to act, so that reads badly:

- `ix view` took an unreadable compass.pid as "not running", spawned the
  detached server, and only then died writing the PID — leaving a visualizer
  with nothing recording it, which `ix view stop` reports as not running and
  no later `ix view` can get past. Reproduced: spawn called, then EISDIR.
- `ix view stop` against a root-owned compass.pid deleted a live server's
  pid/scope/port (unlink needs the directory permission, not the file's) and
  then killed nothing.
- An unreadable compass.scope silently skipped the cross-workspace warning
  and handed back another workspace's graph — the exact confusion that file
  exists to prevent.

`readTextIfPresent` now returns null only for ENOENT and rethrows the rest,
which is what `main` did, without the racy check. `readRunningPort` keeps
its swallow-all policy on purpose and says why: it looks up a URL to print,
not liveness. The scope read also stops treating a zero-length file as a
workspace named "".

The rev change was directionally right with a false rationale. `currentRev`
is read only by `ix status` — incremental skipping runs off the mtime map —
so a rejected rev costs a wrong Revision line, not a re-ingest. Comment and
test header corrected. More to the point the guard was at the last stop: the
value enters at the accumulator, where a bare `>` compares it as a string,
so "9" becomes the max and "10" > "9" is then false and the max walks
backwards. `advanceRev` screens it there, which fixes the max, the
`--format json` contract and the baseline at once. `isRev` is now one
predicate both sides share — they previously sat three lines apart and
disagreed on whether 0 was valid. `previousRev` is looked up lazily; it
parses the whole baseline, and `onCommitted` saves once per deleted file.

Tests: the scope-mismatch branch had no coverage in the whole suite (every
case seeded "*all*" and launched with --all), and the PID test asserted a
cleanup that cannot happen. Both replaced, plus the vacuous NaN case, which
passed against the bug. All five new assertions were checked against
restored mutants: swallow-all resurrects the orphan spawn and the silent
scope warning, and dropping the rev screen lets "9" win the max.

`ix-cli` has always contained a complete `ix patches` — client call, `--limit`,

`@ix/pro` registers a `patches` too. Commander throws on a duplicate command

`--format llm`, but it makes the two implementations' behaviour matter: this one
now uses the same `createClient()` factory Pro's does rather than constructing

auth resolution reaches both.

it is *not* stubbed. A stub for a command that exists in OSS shadows the real
implementation, and because `registerOssCommands` runs first the symptom is
silence rather than a crash — worth pinning.

fix(upgrade): stop comparing compass versions across two unrelated series

`compass/.version` is written by two producers in two different version series,
and recorded no way to tell them apart:

  - the release workflow stamps the bundle it ships with the **Ix** version
    (`0.9.2`), because that bundle is built from system-compass `main` and has no
    ix-compass-dist release number of its own;
  - install.sh and the compass-upgrade path stamp the **ix-compass-dist** release
    they downloaded (`0.3.0`).

`isNewer(compassLatest, compassCurrent)` compared whichever of those happened to
be on disk against the dist series. That is correct only while Ix's numbers are
the larger ones. The first ix-compass-dist tag above the running Ix version — a
v1.0.0, or just a v0.9.2 — makes `isNewer` true and replaces a *newer* bundled
compass with an older dist build. Same failure as #365/#366, reached from the
other end.

It is not only latent. install.sh stamped every install with the latest *dist*
release number regardless of where the compass came from, mislabelling the
release bundle it had just extracted and clobbering the correct stamp the
tarball carried. A v0.9.x install reads `0.2.0` against a dist latest of
`0.3.0`, so `ix upgrade` reports an update and would downgrade the bundle.

The stamp now declares its own provenance and the comparison only runs where it
means something:

    source=release      source=dist
    ix=0.9.3            version=0.3.0
    compass=7f98724

A release bundle is never replaced by a dist download — it was built from `main`
when the CLI was cut, so it is at least as new as any dist release published
before it, and one published after arrives with the next Ix release, which
bundles `main` again. The dist download stays the *repair* path for a missing or
gutted bundle: that still fires, because `getInstalledCompassVersion()` reports
`0.0.0` when `index.html` is absent, which no real release number matches.

A bare number is a legacy stamp (everything up to v0.9.2) and reads as
dist-series — what install.sh wrote, the majority of installs in the wild, and
no less correct than today. New releases carry the explicit form and are immune.

The commit is recorded because system-compass's package.json version is not
maintained against the dist release series — it read 0.2.0 while dist was on
v0.3.0 — so the commit is the only reliable identity a bundle has.

Both installers stop asking ix-compass-dist what it has published. Neither ever
installs from there; `ix upgrade` asks that question, at the one point where it
can also tell which series the installed bundle belongs to.

Fixes #376

fix(upgrade): sweep orphans on every upgrade, not only when one is available

Both sweep calls sit behind "something needs updating" — one inside the CLI
branch, one inside the compass branch, the latter existing precisely as the
fallback for the former. #376 then tightened the compass gate to skip
release-bundled compasses, which is every install from v0.9.3 on. So a user on
the latest CLI with a release compass now runs `ix upgrade` and reclaims
nothing, and an interrupted swap is never restored.

That matters most for this PR: the archives it teaches the sweep about are
multi-MB, and the stated reason for sweeping them is that leaving os.tmpdir()
also left the OS's own cleanup. A sweep that only runs when an update happens
to be available does not deliver that.

One readdir of ~/.ix when there is nothing to do. The calls inside
prepareDownloadDir stay — that is where the sweep-before-scratch ordering is
enforced — and simply find nothing.

fix(upgrade): stage downloads under IX_HOME, not TEMP

#349 is a Windows install that died after extraction because TEMP arrived in
8.3 short form (`[local-path] on a profile named `[local-path] 10`;
the reporter confirmed that pointing TEMP and TMP at a path without a space let
the same install finish. #352 moved install.ps1's scratch off TEMP for that
reason, and said in its own comment that `ix upgrade` still stages through
`os.tmpdir()` — which on Windows is TEMP verbatim — so if the class is real it
is unfixed there.

It is the worse of the two places for it to bite: a failed install leaves a
machine with no Ix on it, but a failed upgrade breaks an install that was
working.

Both download directories move to `IX_HOME`, which comes from USERPROFILE in
its long form, joining the staging and backup directories that were already
there. `mkdirSync(IX_HOME)` first, because a first upgrade after a manual
install may reach this before anything has created it.

Leaving TEMP also leaves the OS's own cleanup, so `sweepUpgradeOrphans` learns
the two new prefixes — otherwise an upgrade killed mid-download parks a
multi-MB archive in ~/.ix forever. They are deliberately `-download-` and not
`-backup-`: `recover()` renames the newest `.cli-backup-*` over the install
directory, and an archive must never be a candidate for that.

**The sweep call had to move above the download.** It sat between the download
and the extract, which was safe only while the scratch lived in os.tmpdir();
now that the sweep reclaims `.cli-download-*`, from that position it would
delete the archive it was about to extract and break every upgrade. Above the
download it also puts an interrupted install back even when the download then
fails, which the old order could not do. The compass branch already had this
ordering.

fix(upgrade): make the sweep-before-download order structural, not a comment

The PR notes the sweep call had to move above the download and says there is
now a test for it. There was not: the two new cases pin which prefixes the
sweep reclaims, but the ordering lived inline in the command action where no
test could reach it. Moving the call back below the download — which breaks
every upgrade on every platform, since the sweep then deletes the archive it
is about to extract — left all 724 tests passing.

Both call sites now go through `prepareDownloadDir()`, which does mkdir,
sweep, mkdtemp in that order and is directly testable. Three cases cover it:
an earlier run's scratch is reclaimed while the new one survives, an
interrupted install is restored before any download happens, and IX_HOME is
created when a manual install never did. Inverting the order inside the
helper fails all three.
